item.title: Vega Island Frozen in Fright
item.summary: The sight of an icy skull-like visage on the Antarctic island could make one’s blood run cold.
item.page_text:
The sight of an icy skull-like visage on the Antarctic island could make one’s blood run cold.
Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island.
These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible.
Above-average temperatures in winter 2026 —particularly in June —were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October , said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”
The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”
The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In a study published in 1982 , scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega.
Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring an overall decline in its mass. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock.
Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, they lost their ship to the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: Strike Damage Confirmed at Giant Saudi Refinery Complex - The Maritime Executive
item.summary: ... ( Sentinel-2 / Copernicus). By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-28 23:25:35. Commercially-available satellite imaging reveals that the Houthi missile ...
item.page_text:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-28 23:25:35
Commercially-available satellite imaging reveals that the Houthi missile strike on the giant oil export hub of Ras Tanura hit a critical component of the site's refining complex.
The unit in question appears to be a cracking unit at the refining complex. Open-source intelligence analysts suggest that the refinery has stopped flaring, a sign that it has shut down or curtailed its operations.
Ras Tanura normally processes up to 550,000 barrels per day, making it one of the largest refineries in Saudi Arabia. The shutdown will reduce throughput for production of diesel, jet fuel, gasoline and bunker fuel, all in short supply on the global market. The timing is poor; most refineries have been running flat-out to capture profits in a period of tight supply conditions, and some have even been extending service intervals to keep running.
The hits on the refinery have not impeded the export of unrefined crude, and Saudi Aramco continues to ship as much as possible out of its Gulf and Red Sea loading terminals. At Ras Tamura and Juaymah, satellite imaging captured nine VLCCs loading simultaneously, enough to carry 18 million barrels at once, according to Bloomberg's Javier Blas. By his calculations, Aramco has fully recovered its prewar crude oil export volumes, and nearly recovered its product exports as well.
According to the Associated Press, there is compelling evidence to suggest that Russian imaging satellites have been used to support Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities. Swiss geospatial consultancy Aurorah Geosignal Intelligence told the AP that there was a "100% match" between the movements of Russian government satellites over Saudi sites and subsequent Houthi missile attacks, including events as recent as October 19.

Houthi and Saudi officials confirmed to the AP that the Houthis have access to Russian satellite intelligence products. Iranian military advisers in Yemen provide both the raw imaging product and  the analysis needed to interpret it, AP's sources said. The officials added that the Houthis also have access to Chinese satellite imaging products.

item.title: Widening oil spill off UAE coast forces beach closures - Roya News
item.summary: Photographs captured on October 24 by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite observation network reveal that the slick has widened over ...
item.page_text:
Note: AI technology was used to generate this article’s audio.
An oil spill originating from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has expanded, according to recent satellite imagery, prompting authorities to close additional beaches amid growing environmental alarms.
Photographs captured on October 24 by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite observation network reveal that the slick has widened over recent days and approached the shores of the northern emirate of Umm Al Quwain, leaving visible dark slicks of crude spreading across the water and reaching the coastline.
The incident unfolds against a backdrop of escalating regional hostilities.
Since the onset of the US-'Israeli' war on Iran, recurrent attacks on commercial vessels across Gulf maritime corridors have sharply increased navigation risks and intensified concerns regarding the conflict's ecological toll.
Data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank indicates that October has been the most severe month for assaults targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters.
On Friday, the UAE stated that operations were actively underway to contain the offshore leak, with the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
While Emirati officials did not officially identify the vessel or specify the exact cause of the discharge, experts told Reuters that the oil originated from a tanker named Gem No.2.
Shipping sources indicated the vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, resulting in an onboard fire that was subsequently extinguished.
In response to the spreading contamination, authorities across several northern emirates enacted strict measures to limit access to coastal zones.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment announced on Friday the temporary closure of all beaches and coastal waterfronts around Umm Al Quwain city. Neighboring Sharjah similarly shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precautionary measure.
"The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Center, told Reuters.
On Saturday, authorities in Ras Al Khaimah, a destination renowned for its luxury resorts and public shores, declared that all beaches across the emirate would remain closed until further notice.
The expanding slick poses hazards to the UAE’s marine ecosystem, which the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) notes is "rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including populations of dolphins and marine turtles.
